title: Laundering dirty money

FATF October 2020 deadline to strengthen Philippine AMLA and AMLC under threat of being deemed a 'threat to the international financial system'

sub_topics: Two serious claims by Sen. Gordon: (1) >US$633M (~₱32B) cash flown in via airports by couriers; (2) ₱20M bribe offered (and refused) by a Filipino family that brought in $283M (~₱15B) to avoid Senate summons
FATF (Paris-based Financial Action Task Force) -- October 2020 deadline
Sanctions risk: banking sanctions making OFW remittances and correspondent-bank relations harder
Money laundering = transacting or attempting to transact cash proceeds of an 'unlawful activity' to make them appear to come from legitimate sources
Kidnapping example: kidnapping is the predicate crime; depositing the ransom in a bank is the separate AMLA crime; bank officials who knew or should have known can be prosecuted separately

AMLA enumerated predicate crimes: kidnapping for ransom, drug trafficking, graft and corruption, plunder, bribery, malversation, carnapping, robbery and extortion, jueteng and masiao, piracy, qualified theft, swindling, smuggling, violations of the Electronic Commerce Act of 2000, hijacking, destructive arson, violations of the Securities Regulation Code, terrorism under RA 9372, terrorism financing under the Terrorism Financing Act of 2012, plus other crimes under special laws
Tax evasion NOT a predicate crime under AMLA (though prosecutable separately under other laws)

Laundering channels: (1) BSP-supervised entities (banks, FX dealers, pawnshops, money changers, remittance companies); (2) IC-supervised entities (insurance, pre-need); (3) SEC-supervised entities (securities dealers, brokers, investment houses, mutual funds); (4) other listed entities
RA 10927 -- casinos (including internet and ship-based) covered for single transactions exceeding ₱5,000,000
Finance Secretary Carlos Dominguez III's proposal: include tax-evasion proceeds as predicate crime; relax bank secrecy law

stances.claim: Senator Gordon's two claims -- a US$633M cash inflow via couriers and a ₱20M bribe offered by a Filipino family that brought in $283M -- are serious and deserve further investigation: the first as a likely AMLA violation (or at least a trigger for AMLA strengthening), and the second as bribery that Sen. Gordon, as a responsible public official, should bring to justice.
stances.rhetorical_move: two-claim recitation with separate doctrinal handling of each

stances.claim: Money laundering is best understood through the predicate-crime structure: an unlawful activity (the predicate) generates 'dirty cash' that is then transacted to appear 'clean,' and these two acts are prosecuted separately under separate statutes -- meaning the kidnappers and the bank officials who knowingly accepted the ransom are distinct categories of offenders.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal explanation through the kidnapping-ransom example

stances.claim: Not all laundering is illegal under AMLA -- only proceeds from the statute's enumerated predicate crimes count, and tax evasion is notably absent from that list (though prosecutable under separate laws), which represents a meaningful gap in the AML regime.
stances.rhetorical_move: exclusion-by-enumeration analysis exposing a doctrinal gap

stances.claim: Congress should heed Finance Secretary Carlos Dominguez III's plea to include tax-evasion proceeds among AMLA predicate crimes and to relax the bank secrecy law -- both to close the doctrinal gap and to fight money laundering and corruption more effectively, with the further benefit of meeting the FATF's October 2020 deadline.
stances.rhetorical_move: executive-attribution endorsement -- agreeing with Dominguez's reform proposal rather than originating it

notable_anecdotes: The kidnapping-ransom worked example -- used as the canonical illustration of how a predicate crime and a money-laundering crime are doctrinally distinct: 'Kidnapping is a crime under our Penal Code. Depositing in a bank the ransom or cash received by the kidnappers is another crime under the AMLA' -- a pedagogically clean classroom example dropped into an opinion column.

The FATF October 2020 deadline as the unspoken urgency behind the entire column: failure to strengthen AMLA could see the Philippines deemed 'a threat to the international financial system,' with downstream sanctions making OFW remittances and correspondent-bank relations more difficult -- a sovereign-reputation stake far beyond the Gordon claims themselves.

RA 10927's specific casino threshold -- ₱5,000,000 per single transaction, including internet and ship-based casinos -- as the newest doctrinal frontier in AMLA coverage and a hint at the Philippine-casino angle in international laundering concerns.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines two claims by Senate blue ribbon committee chair Richard Gordon: (1) more than US$633 million (~₱32 billion) in cash flown in by couriers via Philippine airports, and (2) a ₱20 million bribe offered (and refused) by a Filipino family that allegedly brought in $283 million (~₱15 billion) in exchange for avoiding committee summons. He frames the first as a potential AMLA violation and at least a legislative trigger to strengthen the law and the AMLC ahead of the FATF's October 2020 deadline -- failure to meet which could see the Philippines deemed 'a threat to the international financial system' with consequent banking sanctions affecting OFW remittances and correspondent-bank relations. The second, he argues, is bribery that Sen. Gordon should bring to justice. He then offers a textbook exposition of money laundering: the act of transacting cash proceeds of an 'unlawful activity' to make them appear to come from legitimate sources, illustrated by the kidnapping-ransom example in which the predicate crime (kidnapping) and the laundering crime (depositing the ransom) are prosecuted separately, with bank officials who knowingly accepted the ransom liable for laundering even if uninvolved in the kidnapping. He enumerates AMLA's predicate crimes -- kidnapping for ransom, drug trafficking, graft and corruption, plunder, bribery, malversation, carnapping, robbery and extortion, jueteng and masiao, piracy, qualified theft, swindling, smuggling, e-commerce-act violations, hijacking, destructive arson, securities-regulation violations, terrorism under RA 9372, terrorism financing under the 2012 Act, and other special-law crimes -- and notes that tax evasion is conspicuously absent (though prosecutable separately). He surveys the regulated laundering channels (BSP-supervised banks, FX dealers, pawnshops, money changers, remittance companies; IC-supervised insurance and pre-need; SEC-supervised securities dealers, brokers, investment houses, mutual funds; and casinos including internet and ship-based under RA 10927 for single transactions exceeding ₱5 million). He closes by endorsing Finance Secretary Carlos Dominguez III's reform plea: include tax-evasion proceeds as a predicate crime and relax the bank secrecy law to fight money laundering and corruption more effectively.
